items.questionAndWhy: Can observing small or major rule violations change whether people follow rules, and can rare escalations destabilize group compliance?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers ran a preregistered online experiment with 750 US participants. People could earn more by violating a visual-selection rule, then revised choices after seeing another person's behavior and political affiliation. The team also simulated repeated social influence.
items.whatTheyFound: Major observed violations increased subsequent rule-breaking, particularly when the observed person shared the participant's political affiliation. Minor violations encouraged imitation and sometimes escalation. Simulations suggested rare escalators can amplify noncompliance, while many participants remained rule-followers.
items.whatItMeans: Rule violations are not equally influential: their magnitude and social source matter. The task had monetary incentives but no real-world penalties; simulation cascades are not observed societal breakdowns.
items.streamTitle: Major rule violations spread more readily than rule-following in an online experiment
items.streamSummary: A 750-person experiment found that observing serious rule-breaking increased violations, especially from political in-group members. Simulations suggested rare escalators could amplify noncompliance; real-world sanctions were absent.
items.attribution: Molleman et al. — Proceedings of the Royal Society B

items.questionAndWhy: Which language features distinguish phishing texts from legitimate messages, and could those features make public scam warnings more concrete?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers used systemic-functional linguistics to compare 106 Australian phishing text messages with 16 legitimate messages from organizations commonly impersonated in scams.
items.whatTheyFound: Phishing messages frequently combined urgent time limits, authority cues, instructions, and links. Time markers appeared in about 58% of scam messages and none of the small legitimate comparison set. The study analyzed text features, not recipients' susceptibility or prevention outcomes.
items.whatItMeans: Concrete linguistic examples may strengthen scam-awareness materials, but warning effectiveness and classifier performance still need testing with users and new messages.
items.streamTitle: Phishing texts used urgency and action cues absent from a small legitimate sample
items.streamSummary: A linguistic comparison of 106 scam texts and 16 legitimate texts found frequent urgency, authority, and link-related cues in scams. It did not test whether new warnings reduce victimization.
items.attribution: Kawabata — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

items.questionAndWhy: Does more news coverage of local talent policies produce more favorable public response, or just different levels of engagement?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers built a 2014–2023 panel of 232 Chinese cities, measuring talent-policy news volume and a public-response index combining message sentiment with interaction on a government message board.
items.whatTheyFound: The combined index showed a U-shaped association with coverage, with an estimated turning point near 94 articles per city-year. Separate sentiment measures did not reverse in the observed range; the pattern was mainly about participation, not growing positivity.
items.whatItMeans: More visibility need not mean more favorable sentiment. The analysis is observational and the numerical turning point is sample-specific, not a recommended communication target.
items.streamTitle: More policy coverage tracked public participation, not necessarily favorable sentiment
items.streamSummary: Across 232 Chinese cities, talent-policy media attention had a nonlinear association with a combined response index, while sentiment alone did not show the same reversal. Causality was not established.
items.attribution: Li and Wang — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

items.questionAndWhy: Can a model separate candidate causal triggers from confounded associations when complex biological systems change state?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers developed CauTrigger, combining hierarchical latent-variable modeling and do-calculus. They benchmarked trigger identification and perturbation predictions with synthetic multilayer systems and biological datasets, including single-cell multi-omics and microbiome data.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors reported better trigger identification and modeled responses than comparator approaches in the tested datasets. Real-data applications prioritized hypotheses and used in-silico perturbations; they did not establish that every inferred trigger would work in a laboratory intervention.
items.whatItMeans: Hierarchical causal decomposition is a promising modeling approach, but identification assumptions and prospective experimental validation remain decisive. Biological benchmarks do not directly validate behavioral or social causal models.
items.streamTitle: CauTrigger modeled candidate causes across biological regulatory layers
items.streamSummary: A Nature Methods study introduced hierarchical latent-variable causal modeling and reported improvements on synthetic and biological benchmarks. In-silico perturbations nominate testable triggers, not proven interventions.

items.questionAndWhy: How are language models being used to combine clinical notes with structured health records for prediction?
items.whatTheyDid: A systematic review screened 641 publications and included 57 studies of LLM-enabled multimodal prediction using electronic health records. It grouped methods into text embeddings, information extraction, and text fusion.
items.whatTheyFound: Across included comparisons, multimodal approaches reported an average 6.4% performance gain over single-modality models. Studies differed in tasks, datasets, baselines, and evaluation, and the review identified interpretability, sample size, and compute costs as limitations.
items.whatItMeans: Language models can help represent unstructured records, but the average gain should not be treated as a universal effect or proof of safer clinical decisions. External and prospective validation remain important.
items.streamTitle: Review finds modest average gains from combining clinical text and structured records
items.streamSummary: A systematic review retained 57 of 641 studies and found a reported average 6.4% improvement for LLM-enabled multimodal prediction. Heterogeneous studies and deployment limits constrain the claim.
items.attribution: Kaster et al. — npj Digital Medicine (systematic review)

items.questionAndWhy: Can NATO reduce delays between receiving targeting information and making decisions by connecting allied systems and testing AI support?
items.whatTheyDid: NATO ACT announced Next Generation Targeting testing at DiBaX26 with operators from 11 allies, more than 6,000 simulated targets and more than 100 live targets. Operators will compare a baseline targeting cycle with an AI-assisted cycle.
items.whatTheyFound: The stated objective is to cut information-to-decision time by more than half while measuring accuracy, workload, and decision quality. The October 21 announcement describes planned tests and human engagement controls, not results showing that the goal was achieved.
items.whatItMeans: A paired workflow test with time, accuracy, and workload measures is a stronger evidence plan than a demonstration alone. Report achieved outcomes separately from the 50% target and preserve the human-decision boundary.
items.streamTitle: NATO plans a baseline-versus-AI test of targeting decision speed
items.streamSummary: At DiBaX26, NATO plans to test a targeting workflow across 11 allies using simulated and live targets, aiming for more than 50% less decision time. No achieved speed or accuracy results were published.
items.attribution: NATO Allied Command Transformation — official October 21 report

items.questionAndWhy: How have higher-education institutions responded to generative-AI plagiarism when the technology and its definition are changing?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers compared publicly available government and university policy documents, including responses from 359 Japanese universities, with the Chinese higher-education policy setting.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors described extensive institutional silence in China and a Japanese approach they summarize as 'No Copy + Exceptions.' Their assessment of institutional inertia is interpretive policy analysis, not measured evidence that one approach reduces plagiarism.
items.whatItMeans: Policy ambiguity need not prevent explicit rules and exception handling. Compare implementability, appeal procedures, faculty autonomy, and outcomes before concluding which governance model works best.
items.streamTitle: China–Japan policy comparison highlights differing responses to AI plagiarism
items.streamSummary: A document-based comparison of Chinese policy and 359 Japanese universities identified institutional silence and a Japanese 'No Copy + Exceptions' approach. It did not test which policy prevents plagiarism.
items.attribution: Zhang and Chen — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

items.questionAndWhy: What do emergency-management practitioners see as barriers and enablers to adopting generative AI during crises?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers interviewed Chinese emergency-management experts and used intuitionistic fuzzy DEMATEL analysis to organize perceived relationships among technology acceptance, decision processes, context, risk and trust, and individual factors.
items.whatTheyFound: In the elicited expert model, contextual and decision-process factors were ranked as influential, with organizational support, trust, and self-efficacy described as enabling conditions. These are expert perceptions and modeled influence links, not tested adoption interventions or measured crisis outcomes.
items.whatItMeans: Emergency AI integration is an organizational and human decision problem as well as a technical one. Validate the identified factors with observed adoption, error rates, and operational performance before treating ranked links as causal levers.
items.streamTitle: Emergency managers ranked organizational context as central to AI adoption
items.streamSummary: Expert interviews and fuzzy DEMATEL analysis in China identified contextual and decision-process barriers to generative-AI adoption in crises. The findings are perceived relationships, not demonstrated effects.
items.attribution: Fei, Sun and Sun — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

items.questionAndWhy: Can science-fiction films support students' reflection on technological, societal, and ethical futures?
items.whatTheyDid: A German university seminar used science-fiction films as discussion material. Researchers examined students' reflective writing and conducted an exploratory pre/post comparison of reported climate-change and planetary-health perceptions.
items.whatTheyFound: Qualitative writing indicated engagement with complex scenarios, values, and future-oriented questions. Quantitative comparisons showed no statistically significant change between the two measurement points.
items.whatItMeans: Films may be useful prompts for discussion and scenario exploration, but the study did not demonstrate improvements in tested attitudes, critical thinking, or long-term learning.
items.streamTitle: Science-fiction seminars prompted reflection without measurable attitude change
items.streamSummary: A mixed-methods university study found useful qualitative reflection around science-fiction films, while exploratory pre/post climate and planetary-health measures did not change significantly.
items.attribution: Lüdorf, Ehlers and Nitsche — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
